content:
Textual authority does not establish intellectual immobility
Treating a sacred text as authoritative constrains inquiry, sometimes severely. It does not by itself show that adherents cannot develop interpretations, learn new facts or improve their conduct. The sweeping foil needs a more accurate account of the tradition before it can demonstrate a uniquely rationalist virtue.

quote: which is about confessing sins—not avoiding sins
content:
The religious foil omits repentance’s demand for change
A ritual confession can become empty performance, but Judaism does not define repentance as reciting guilt while planning to repeat the offense. Maimonides explicitly requires abandoning wrongdoing and resolving against its recurrence. Criticize the observed gap between doctrine and practice if evidence supports it; the doctrine itself already contains the author’s central demand for improvement.
Maimonides, Repentance 2:2

quote: what you plan to do about it
content:
Improvement is more useful than a ritual of inferiority
Naming a mistake and changing a relevant behavior is a defensible standard for progress. Neither recurrent confession nor an elevated self-image establishes that change. Specify the capacity being improved and measure it: motion, effort and confidence can all increase while performance gets worse.
